category.name: Statistics
category.description: Probability, distributions, descriptive statistics, inference, regression and time series.

notes.title: Type I and Type II Errors

questions.text: What does a correlation coefficient of $r = -1$ imply?
options: A perfect positive linear relationship
No linear relationship
A perfect negative linear relationship
A weak negative linear relationship
questions.explanation: $r = -1$ means every point lies exactly on a straight line with negative slope. The sign gives the direction and $|r|$ gives the strength.

questions.text: In an ordinary least-squares regression that includes an intercept, what do the residuals always sum to?
options: One
Zero
The sum of the observed responses
The residual standard error
questions.explanation: The least-squares normal equation for the intercept forces $\sum e_i = 0$. As a result the fitted line passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$.

questions.text: Two variables have covariance 12, and their standard deviations are 3 and 5. What is their correlation?
questions.explanation: $r = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{s_X s_Y} = \frac{12}{3 \times 5} = 0.8$. Standardising by the SDs makes the correlation unit-free, unlike the covariance.

questions.text: Heights are recorded in centimetres and then converted to inches. What happens to their correlation with weight?
options: It is multiplied by 2.54
It is divided by 2.54
It does not change
It changes sign
questions.explanation: Correlation does not change under positive linear changes of scale or location in either variable. Covariance does change with the units.

questions.text: What does a correlation coefficient of $r = 0$ imply?
options: A strong positive relationship
The variables are independent
No linear relationship between the variables
A perfect positive correlation
questions.explanation: $r$ measures only linear association. Variables can be strongly related in a non-linear way, such as $y = x^2$ on a symmetric range, and still have $r = 0$, so zero correlation does not imply independence.

questions.text: In simple linear regression, what does the slope represent?
options: The predicted value of the response when x is 0
The predicted change in the response for a one-unit increase in x
The proportion of variation in the response explained
The average size of the residuals
questions.explanation: In $\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x$, $b_1$ is the change in $\hat{y}$ per unit of $x$. The intercept $b_0$ is the prediction at $x = 0$.

questions.text: What does multicollinearity mean in a multiple regression model?
options: Two or more predictors are highly correlated with each other
The response is highly correlated with the predictors
The residuals are not normally distributed
The regression coefficients are all close to zero
questions.explanation: Correlated predictors make it hard to separate their individual effects. This inflates coefficient standard errors and makes the estimates unstable. A strong predictor–response correlation is desirable.

questions.text: A simple linear regression has correlation $r = -0.6$ between x and y. What is $R^2$?
questions.explanation: In simple linear regression $R^2 = r^2 = (-0.6)^2 = 0.36$, so 36% of the variation in y is explained by x. $R^2$ cannot be negative.

questions.text: A correlation coefficient of about 0.9 indicates:
options: No linear correlation
A weak positive linear correlation
A strong positive linear correlation
A strong negative linear correlation
questions.explanation: Values of $r$ near +1 mean the points lie close to an upward-sloping line. The sign gives the direction, so 0.9 is positive.

questions.text: In simple linear regression, what does the intercept represent?
options: The predicted change in the response for a one-unit increase in x
The predicted value of the response when x equals 0
The residual sum of squares of the model
The correlation between x and the response
questions.explanation: $b_0 = \hat{y}$ at $x = 0$. It is only meaningful if $x = 0$ is within or near the range of the observed data.

questions.text: Which is a standard assumption of the classical linear regression model?
options: The predictors must be normally distributed
The relationship between x and y is non-linear
The errors are independent with constant variance and, for exact inference, normal
The response must take only the values 0 and 1
questions.explanation: The usual assumptions are linearity, independent errors, constant error variance and normal errors for t and F inference. The predictors themselves need not be normal, and a 0/1 response calls for logistic regression.

questions.text: Which pattern most clearly signals that a multiple regression model is overfitting?
options: High $R^2$ on the training data but poor accuracy on new data
Low $R^2$ on both the training data and new data
Normally distributed residuals with constant variance
Similar prediction error on training data and new data
questions.explanation: An overfit model learns noise in the training sample, so it fits that sample well but generalises poorly. Low $R^2$ everywhere points to underfitting instead.

questions.text: What does the Durbin–Watson test assess in a regression model?
options: Multicollinearity among the predictors
Constant variance of the residuals
Autocorrelation (lack of independence) in the residuals
Whether the coefficients are jointly significant
questions.explanation: The Durbin–Watson statistic tests for first-order autocorrelation in residuals, which is common with time-ordered data. Values near 2 suggest no autocorrelation.

questions.text: The p-value for the slope in a simple linear regression is 0.01. What can you conclude at the 5% level?
options: There is significant evidence that the true slope is not zero
The predictor has no effect on the response
The model's $R^2$ must be high
The residuals are normally distributed
questions.explanation: The p-value tests $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$, and $0.01 < 0.05$ rejects it. A significant slope can still come with a low $R^2$, and it says nothing about the residual assumptions.

questions.text: What does it mean if the residuals of a regression model are heteroscedastic?
options: The residuals have constant variance
The spread of the residuals changes with the fitted values or predictors
The residuals are normally distributed
The residuals are correlated with each other over time
questions.explanation: Heteroscedasticity means non-constant error variance, often seen as a funnel shape in a residuals-versus-fitted plot. Correlation over time is autocorrelation, a different problem.

questions.text: What kind of response variable is standard logistic regression designed for?
options: A continuous, unbounded variable
A binary variable such as yes/no or 0/1
A count with no upper limit
A normally distributed variable
questions.explanation: Logistic regression models the probability of the outcome being 1 through the log-odds, $\ln\frac{p}{1-p} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$. Unbounded counts are usually modelled with Poisson regression.

questions.text: In regression, what does the coefficient of determination $R^2$ represent?
options: The proportion of variance in the response explained by the model
The slope of the fitted regression line
The mean of the residuals
The total variance of the predictor
questions.explanation: $R^2 = 1 - SSE/SST$, the share of the total variation in $y$ that the fitted model accounts for. It ranges from 0 to 1 for least squares with an intercept.

questions.text: What does a high variance inflation factor (VIF) indicate?
options: The predictor explains most of the variation in the response
The predictor is strongly correlated with the other predictors
The residuals are normally distributed
The model fits the data poorly
questions.explanation: $VIF_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2)$, where $R_j^2$ comes from regressing predictor $j$ on the other predictors. Values above about 5–10 signal problematic multicollinearity.

questions.text: What does a negative correlation coefficient imply?
options: As one variable increases, the other tends to increase
As one variable increases, the other tends to decrease
There is no relationship between the variables
The variables move in perfect unison
questions.explanation: A negative $r$ means high values of one variable go with low values of the other. "Tends to" matters: unless $r = -1$, the pattern is not exact.

questions.text: What does adjusted $R^2$ account for that ordinary $R^2$ does not?
options: The correlation among the predictors
The number of predictors relative to the sample size
The significance of each regression coefficient
The normality of the residuals
questions.explanation: Ordinary $R^2$ never decreases when a predictor is added. Adjusted $R^2 = 1 - (1 - R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-p-1}$ penalises extra predictors, so it can fall when a useless variable is added.

questions.text: A model with $p = 4$ predictors fitted to $n = 25$ observations has $R^2 = 0.80$. What is the adjusted $R^2$?
The correlation between x and y is 0.5, with $s_x = 2$ and $s_y = 10$. What is the least-squares slope for predicting y from x?
questions.explanation: $b_1 = r\frac{s_y}{s_x} = 0.5 \times \frac{10}{2} = 2.5$. Swapping the SDs gives 0.1, which is the slope for predicting x from y.

questions.text: A fitted line has slope 2.5, and the data have $\bar{x} = 4$ and $\bar{y} = 50$. What is the predicted y at x = 6?
questions.explanation: The intercept is $b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1\bar{x} = 50 - 2.5 \times 4 = 40$, so $\hat{y} = 40 + 2.5 \times 6 = 55$.

questions.text: In a logistic regression, a predictor has coefficient $\beta = 0.693$. What happens to the odds of the outcome when that predictor increases by one unit?
options: They increase by 0.693
They roughly double
They roughly halve
The probability increases by 69.3 percentage points
questions.explanation: The odds ratio is $e^{\beta} = e^{0.693} \approx 2$, so the odds are multiplied by about 2. The coefficient acts on the log-odds, not directly on the probability.

questions.text: Two variables have a strong monotonic but curved relationship, with one extreme outlier. Which correlation measure is most suitable?
options: Pearson correlation
Spearman rank correlation
Covariance
Coefficient of determination
questions.explanation: Spearman's $\rho$ is Pearson's $r$ computed on ranks. It captures any monotonic relationship and is resistant to outliers, while Pearson's $r$ measures only linear association.

questions.text: A study finds that cities with more ice-cream sales have more drownings. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
options: Ice-cream consumption causes drowning
Drowning causes higher ice-cream sales
A lurking variable, such as hot weather, may drive both
The correlation must be a calculation error
questions.explanation: Correlation does not establish causation. Hot weather raises both ice-cream sales and swimming, and a confounder like this can produce a strong correlation without any direct causal link.

questions.text: Which measure is most appropriate for comparing the relative spread of datasets measured in different units?
options: Standard deviation
Variance
Range
Coefficient of variation
questions.explanation: The coefficient of variation $s/\bar{x}$ is unit-free, so it can compare, say, spread in heights (cm) with spread in weights (kg). The other measures carry the units of the data.

questions.text: What is the relationship between the variance and the standard deviation?
options: The variance is the square root of the standard deviation
The variance is the square of the standard deviation
The variance is twice the standard deviation
The variance is the standard deviation divided by n
questions.explanation: The standard deviation is defined as $\sqrt{\text{variance}}$, which puts it back in the original units of the data.

questions.text: What is the main difference between a sample mean and a population mean?
options: The sample mean is always larger than the population mean
The sample mean is computed from a subset, while the population mean uses every member
The population mean can only be used for hypothesis testing
The sample mean ignores outliers, while the population mean does not
questions.explanation: $\bar{x}$ is a statistic computed from observed data and varies from sample to sample. $\mu$ is a fixed, usually unknown parameter that $\bar{x}$ estimates.

questions.text: What is the median of a dataset?
options: The most frequent value in the dataset
The middle value of the sorted data, or the mean of the two middle values
The arithmetic average of all values in the dataset
The midpoint between the minimum and the maximum
questions.explanation: Sort the data and take the central value; with an even count, average the two central values. The midpoint of the min and max is the midrange.

questions.text: What happens to the standard error of the mean as the sample size increases?
options: It increases
It decreases
It stays the same
It increases and then decreases
questions.explanation: $SE = \sigma/\sqrt{n}$, so larger samples give more precise estimates of the mean. Quadrupling $n$ halves the standard error.

questions.text: You want to show how many cars of each model are in a parking lot. Which graph is most appropriate?
options: Line graph
Histogram
Bar chart
Scatter plot
questions.explanation: Car model is a categorical variable, and a bar chart displays the count for each category. Histograms are for binned numerical data.

questions.text: Which of the following is a continuous variable?
options: The number of heads in 10 coin flips
The outcome of rolling a die
The height of students in a class
The number of students in a class
questions.explanation: Height can take any value in an interval. The other three are counts or outcomes with a finite set of possible values, so they are discrete.

questions.text: Which measure of centre is least sensitive to outliers?
options: Mean
Median
Midrange
Weighted mean
questions.explanation: The median depends only on the middle of the sorted data, so moving an extreme value does not change it. The mean and midrange both shift with extreme values.

questions.text: What does the interquartile range (IQR) measure?
options: The distance between the largest and smallest values
The spread of the middle 50% of the data, $Q_3 - Q_1$
The average squared distance from the mean
The distance between the mean and the median
questions.explanation: The IQR is the difference between the third and first quartiles, so it ignores the most extreme 25% at each end. The first option is the range.

questions.text: What is a box plot mainly used for?
options: Showing the relationship between two numerical variables
Summarising a distribution with its median, quartiles, whiskers and outliers
Showing the share of each category in a whole
Showing how a variable changes over time
questions.explanation: A box plot draws the box from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$ with a line at the median, extends whiskers to the most extreme points within $1.5 \times IQR$, and plots points beyond as potential outliers.

questions.text: Which of the following is a measure of central tendency?
options: Standard deviation
Variance
Median
Range
questions.explanation: Mean, median and mode describe where the data are centred. Standard deviation, variance and range describe spread.

questions.text: Which statistic measures the typical spread of data around the mean, in the original units?
options: Mean
Median
Standard deviation
Mode
questions.explanation: The standard deviation is the square root of the average squared deviation from the mean. The variance measures the same spread but in squared units.

questions.text: A dataset is strongly right-skewed. Which measure of centre is pulled furthest towards the long tail?
options: Mean
Median
Mode
10% trimmed mean
questions.explanation: The mean uses every value, so a few large values pull it up. The trimmed mean discards the extremes and the median and mode are barely affected.

questions.text: Test scores have mean 70 and standard deviation 10. What is the z-score of a score of 85?
questions.explanation: $z = (x - \mu)/\sigma = (85 - 70)/10 = 1.5$, so the score is 1.5 standard deviations above the mean.

questions.text: Which of the following is not a measure of dispersion?
options: Variance
Standard deviation
Mean
Interquartile range
questions.explanation: The mean measures the centre of the data. Variance, standard deviation and IQR all describe how spread out the values are.

questions.text: For the data 2, 3, 3, 4, 48, what are the mean and median?
options: Mean 12, median 3
Mean 3, median 12
Mean 12, median 4
Mean 3, median 3
questions.explanation: The mean is $60/5 = 12$ and the median (third sorted value) is 3. The single outlier 48 drags the mean far above every other value while the median ignores it.

questions.text: If the mean and median of a unimodal dataset are equal, the distribution is most likely:
options: Left-skewed
Right-skewed
Symmetric
questions.explanation: In a symmetric distribution the mean and median coincide, while skew pulls the mean towards the long tail. Equality is not proof of symmetry, but it is what you would expect.

questions.text: How many modes does the dataset 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4 have?
options: None
One
Two
Four
questions.explanation: The values 2 and 3 both occur twice, more often than any other value, so the dataset is bimodal with modes 2 and 3.

questions.text: What is the population standard deviation of the data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9?
questions.explanation: The mean is 5 and the squared deviations sum to $9+1+1+1+0+0+4+16 = 32$. Dividing by $n = 8$ gives variance 4, so $\sigma = 2$. Dividing by $n - 1 = 7$ would give the sample SD, 2.14.

questions.text: In a bimodal distribution, how many peaks does the histogram have?
options: One
Two
Three
None
questions.explanation: Bimodal means two distinct peaks. This often means two subgroups are mixed together, such as the heights of adult men and women.

questions.text: Which variable is categorical?
options: Height of students
Number of hours worked
Type of fruit sold
Temperature of a city
questions.explanation: Fruit type places each observation in a named group with no numerical meaning. The other three are numerical measurements.

questions.text: A distribution has a long tail to the right. What is the typical relationship between the mean and the median?
options: The mean is less than the median
The mean equals the median
The mean is greater than the median
The mean and median have no typical ordering
questions.explanation: The large values in the right tail pull the mean upwards while the median stays near the bulk of the data, so typically mean > median.

questions.text: Which plot is most useful for showing the relationship between two continuous variables?
options: Pie chart
Histogram
Scatter plot
Box plot
questions.explanation: A scatter plot puts one variable on each axis, so it shows direction, form, strength and outliers in the relationship. Histograms and box plots show one variable at a time.

questions.text: You know only the number of households and one summary of their incomes, and you need to recover the total income. Which summary must it be?
options: Mean
Median
Mode
Interquartile range
questions.explanation: Total $= n \times \bar{x}$, so only the mean lets you reconstruct the sum. The median is often better for a typical household when incomes are skewed, but it does not determine the total.

questions.text: Which measure of spread is least affected by outliers?
options: Range
Variance
Standard deviation
Interquartile range
questions.explanation: The IQR uses only the quartiles, so extreme values at either end do not change it. The range depends entirely on the extremes, and the variance squares large deviations.

questions.text: If every value in a dataset is multiplied by 3, what happens to the mean?
options: It stays the same
It decreases by 3
It increases by 3
It is multiplied by 3
questions.explanation: The mean is linear: $\text{mean}(3x) = 3\,\text{mean}(x)$. The standard deviation is also multiplied by 3, and the variance by 9.

questions.text: Which measure of centre is usually most appropriate for a strongly skewed distribution?
options: Mean
Mode
Median
Midrange
questions.explanation: The median is resistant to the long tail, so it represents a typical value better. This is why median income or median house price is usually reported.

questions.text: Which variable is ordinal?
options: Brand of phone owned
Exact weight in kilograms
Customer satisfaction rated low, medium or high
Country of birth
questions.explanation: Ordinal categories have a natural order but no fixed distance between levels. Brand and country are nominal (no order), and weight is a continuous numerical variable.

questions.text: What is the range of the dataset 4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42?
questions.explanation: Range = maximum − minimum = $42 - 4 = 38$. The value 15.5 is the median.

questions.text: What is the mode of the dataset 5, 7, 7, 9, 9, 9, 11?
questions.explanation: 9 appears three times, more often than any other value. The mean of the data is about 8.14.

questions.text: Using the notes' quartile method, what is the IQR of 3, 5, 5, 5, 8, 10, 10, 10, 14?
questions.explanation: With $n = 9$, $Q_1$ sits at position $1 + 8(0.25) = 3$, giving 5, and $Q_3$ at position $1 + 8(0.75) = 7$, giving 10. So $IQR = 10 - 5 = 5$. The range would be 11.

questions.text: If you add 10 to every value in a dataset, what happens to the standard deviation?
options: It increases by 10
It decreases by 10
It stays the same
It is multiplied by 10
questions.explanation: Adding a constant shifts every value and the mean by the same amount, so the deviations from the mean, and therefore the SD, do not change.

questions.text: Which kind of data is a pie chart best suited to?
options: Shares of a whole across a few categories
A continuous variable such as height
The relationship between two numerical variables
Values recorded at regular points in time
questions.explanation: A pie chart shows how a total is split among categories, and it works best with only a few. Continuous data suit histograms, bivariate data suit scatter plots, and time series suit line graphs.

questions.text: Why does the sample variance divide by $n - 1$ instead of $n$?
options: To make the variance less sensitive to outliers
To make it an unbiased estimator of the population variance
To convert the variance into the original units
To make the variance equal to the squared mean
questions.explanation: Deviations are measured from $\bar{x}$ rather than the unknown $\mu$, which makes them slightly too small. Dividing by $n - 1$ corrects this, so $E[s^2] = \sigma^2$.

questions.text: What is the sample variance of the data 1, 2, 3, 4, 5?
questions.explanation: The mean is 3 and the squared deviations sum to $4+1+0+1+4 = 10$. Dividing by $n - 1 = 4$ gives 2.5. Dividing by $n = 5$ gives the population variance, 2.0.

questions.text: A distribution has excess kurtosis well above zero. What does this indicate compared with a normal distribution?
options: It is skewed to the left
It has heavier tails, so extreme values are more common
It has lighter tails, so extreme values are rarer
It has a larger standard deviation
questions.explanation: Kurtosis measures tail weight. A normal distribution has kurtosis 3, which is excess kurtosis 0. Positive excess (leptokurtic) means heavier tails, as with financial returns. Kurtosis says nothing about scale or skew direction.

questions.text: What is the probability of getting exactly two heads when flipping three fair coins?
questions.explanation: There are $2^3 = 8$ equally likely outcomes and $\binom{3}{2} = 3$ of them (HHT, HTH, THH) contain exactly two heads, so the probability is $3/8$.

questions.text: Which statement is a consequence derived from Kolmogorov's axioms rather than one of the axioms themselves?
options: $P(A) \ge 0$ for every event $A$
$P(S) = 1$ for the whole sample space $S$
$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$ for disjoint $A$ and $B$
$P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$ for every event $A$
questions.explanation: The axioms are non-negativity, normalisation and additivity for disjoint events. The complement rule follows from them because $A$ and $A^c$ are disjoint and together make up $S$.

questions.text: The probability of an event A given that event B has occurred is known as:
options: Joint probability
Marginal probability
Conditional probability
Complementary probability
questions.explanation: $P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B)/P(B)$ restricts attention to outcomes where $B$ happened. Joint probability $P(A \cap B)$ does not condition on anything.

questions.text: Which statement is true for two independent events A and B with positive probabilities?
options: The probability of their intersection is zero
Knowing that B occurred changes the probability of A
The probability of their intersection is the product of their probabilities
The probability of their union is the sum of their probabilities
questions.explanation: Independence means $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$. A zero intersection describes mutually exclusive events, which are in fact dependent when both have positive probability.

questions.text: If a fair die is rolled, what is the probability of getting a number greater than 4?
questions.explanation: Only 5 and 6 are greater than 4, so the probability is $2/6 = 1/3$.

questions.text: What does Bayes' theorem let you compute?
options: $P(A \mid B)$ from $P(B \mid A)$, the prior $P(A)$ and $P(B)$
$P(A \cap B)$ for events that are known to be independent
$P(A \cup B)$ for events that are mutually exclusive
$P(A^c)$ from the probability of the event $A$
questions.explanation: Bayes' theorem reverses a conditional probability: $P(A \mid B) = P(B \mid A)P(A)/P(B)$. It is how a prior belief is updated after observing evidence $B$.

questions.text: If $P(A) = 0.4$ and $P(B) = 0.5$, and A and B are independent, what is $P(A \cap B)$?
questions.explanation: For independent events $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.4 \times 0.5 = 0.2$. Adding the probabilities (0.9) would give the union of disjoint events instead.

questions.text: Two events A and B are mutually exclusive with $P(A) = 0.3$ and $P(B) = 0.4$. What is $P(A \cup B)$?
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together, so $P(A \cap B) = 0$ and $P(A \cup B) = 0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7$. The value 0.58 would apply only if the events were independent.

questions.text: If $P(A \mid B) = 0.8$ and $P(B) = 0.5$, what is $P(A \cap B)$?
questions.explanation: The multiplication rule gives $P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)P(B) = 0.8 \times 0.5 = 0.4$.

questions.text: A random variable X takes only the values 1, 2 and 3. Which assignment of $P(X=1), P(X=2), P(X=3)$ is a valid probability distribution?
questions.explanation: Probabilities must be non-negative and sum to 1. Only 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.5 = 1 satisfies both; the second option sums to 1 but contains a negative value.

questions.text: What is the complement of an event A?
options: The event that A and some other event both occur
The event that A occurs at least once in repeated trials
The set of all outcomes in the sample space that are not in A
The event that A occurs given that another event occurred
questions.explanation: The complement $A^c$ contains exactly the outcomes where $A$ does not happen, so $P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$.

questions.text: One card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that it is an Ace or a King?
questions.explanation: There are 4 Aces and 4 Kings and no card is both, so the events are disjoint: $4/52 + 4/52 = 8/52 = 2/13$.

questions.text: If $P(A) = 0.6$, $P(B) = 0.5$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.3$, what is $P(A \cup B)$?
questions.explanation: The general addition rule subtracts the overlap that would otherwise be counted twice: $0.6 + 0.5 - 0.3 = 0.8$.

questions.text: In Bayes' theorem, what is the term for $P(B \mid A)$, the probability of the evidence B given the hypothesis A?
options: Prior probability
Marginal probability
Posterior probability
Likelihood
questions.explanation: $P(B \mid A)$ is the likelihood. The prior is $P(A)$, the posterior is $P(A \mid B)$, and the marginal probability of the evidence is $P(B)$.

questions.text: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 7?
questions.explanation: Six of the 36 equally likely ordered pairs sum to 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1). So the probability is $6/36 = 1/6$.

questions.text: What is the probability of drawing a red card from a standard 52-card deck?
questions.explanation: Hearts and diamonds are red, giving 26 red cards out of 52, so the probability is $26/52 = 1/2$.

questions.text: $P(A) = 0.3$, $P(B) = 0.5$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.15$. Are A and B independent?
options: Yes, because $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$
No, because $P(A \cap B)$ is not zero
No, because $P(A) + P(B)$ is less than 1
It cannot be decided without $P(A \cup B)$
questions.explanation: $P(A)P(B) = 0.3 \times 0.5 = 0.15$, which equals $P(A \cap B)$, so the defining condition for independence holds. A non-zero intersection only rules out mutual exclusivity.

questions.text: If the probability of drawing a blue marble from a bag is 0.3, what is the probability of not drawing a blue marble?
questions.explanation: By the complement rule, $P(\text{not blue}) = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7$.

questions.text: A and B are independent with $P(A) = 0.3$ and $P(B) = 0.6$. What is $P(A \cup B)$?
questions.explanation: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A)P(B) = 0.3 + 0.6 - 0.18 = 0.72$. Simply adding (0.9) double-counts the overlap.

questions.text: Which of the following is not an example of a conditional probability?
options: The probability of drawing a red card given the first card drawn was black
The probability of rolling a 6 on a single fair die
The probability of being late to work given that it is raining
The probability of passing a test given that you studied
questions.explanation: Rolling a 6 is an unconditional probability (1/6). Every other option restricts attention to cases where some other event has already happened.

questions.text: Machine M1 makes 60% of a factory's parts with a 2% defect rate; machine M2 makes the other 40% with a 5% defect rate. What is the probability that a randomly chosen part is defective?
questions.explanation: By the law of total probability, $P(D) = 0.6 \times 0.02 + 0.4 \times 0.05 = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032$. Averaging the two rates (0.035) ignores the different production shares.

questions.text: In a factory, M1 makes 60% of parts (2% defective) and M2 makes 40% (5% defective). Given that a part is defective, what is the probability it came from M2?
questions.explanation: Bayes' theorem gives $P(M2 \mid D) = \frac{0.4 \times 0.05}{0.032} = \frac{0.020}{0.032} = 0.625$. The prior share 0.40 rises because M2 has the higher defect rate.

questions.text: A disease affects 1% of a population. A test detects it 99% of the time and gives a false positive 5% of the time. Approximately what is the probability that a person who tests positive has the disease?
questions.explanation: $P(D \mid +) = \frac{0.01 \times 0.99}{0.01 \times 0.99 + 0.99 \times 0.05} = \frac{0.0099}{0.0594} \approx 0.17$. Because the disease is rare, false positives outnumber true positives.

questions.text: A point is chosen uniformly at random inside the unit square $[0,1] \times [0,1]$. What is the probability that its coordinates satisfy $x + y < 1$?
questions.explanation: In geometric probability the answer is a ratio of areas. The region $x + y < 1$ is the triangle below the diagonal, with area $1/2$, out of a total area of 1.

questions.text: Which statement describes a continuous uniform distribution on the interval $[a, b]$?
options: Its density is constant on $[a, b]$, so equal-length subintervals are equally likely
Its density peaks at the midpoint $(a+b)/2$ and falls towards the ends
It can only describe variables that take a finite number of values
It is skewed to the right, with a long tail towards $b$
questions.explanation: The uniform density is $1/(b-a)$ everywhere on $[a, b]$, so the probability of a subinterval depends only on its length. It is symmetric, with mean $(a+b)/2$.

questions.text: If X follows a log-normal distribution, which statement is true?
options: $\ln X$ is normally distributed and X takes only positive values
X is symmetric, so its mean equals its median
X can take negative values in its left tail
$e^X$ is normally distributed and X is bounded above
questions.explanation: By definition $X = e^Y$ with $Y$ normal, so $X > 0$. The distribution is right-skewed, so its mean exceeds its median. This is why it is used for prices and incomes.

questions.text: Which property holds for a Poisson distribution with parameter $\lambda$?
options: Its mean and its variance both equal $\lambda$
Its variance equals $\lambda^2$
It applies to continuous random variables
It counts successes in a fixed number of trials
questions.explanation: For $X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$, $E[X] = \text{Var}(X) = \lambda$. Counting successes in a fixed number of trials describes the binomial distribution.

questions.text: Which property characterises the exponential distribution?
options: It has a constant hazard rate, so it is memoryless
It is symmetric about its mean $1/\lambda$
It is defined for negative as well as positive values
Its variance equals its mean $1/\lambda$
questions.explanation: The exponential distribution satisfies $P(T > s + t \mid T > s) = P(T > t)$ because its failure rate $\lambda$ is constant. Its variance is $1/\lambda^2$, not $1/\lambda$.

questions.text: A help desk receives calls independently at an average rate of 4 per hour. Which distribution best models the number of calls in one hour?
options: Normal distribution
Poisson distribution
Exponential distribution
Geometric distribution
questions.explanation: Counts of independent events occurring at a constant average rate in a fixed interval follow a Poisson distribution, here with $\lambda = 4$. The exponential would model the waiting time between calls.

questions.text: For $X \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p)$ with fixed $0 < p < 1$, what happens to the shape of the distribution as n grows large?
options: It becomes more and more skewed
It becomes approximately normal
It becomes approximately uniform
It becomes approximately exponential
questions.explanation: A binomial count is a sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli trials, so by the central limit theorem it approaches $N(np, np(1-p))$. A common rule of thumb is $np \ge 10$ and $n(1-p) \ge 10$.

questions.text: For a normal distribution, approximately what percentage of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean?
questions.explanation: The empirical rule gives about 68% within $\pm 1\sigma$, 95% within $\pm 2\sigma$ and 99.7% within $\pm 3\sigma$.

questions.text: If $X \sim \text{Binomial}(10, 0.3)$, what are its mean and variance?
options: Mean 3, variance 2.1
Mean 3, variance 3
Mean 3, variance 0.21
Mean 0.3, variance 2.1
questions.explanation: For a binomial, $E[X] = np = 10 \times 0.3 = 3$ and $\text{Var}(X) = np(1-p) = 10 \times 0.3 \times 0.7 = 2.1$.

questions.text: What does the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) state?
options: Any sufficiently large sample of raw data is normally distributed
The sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches normal as n grows
The population mean of any variable is normally distributed
Larger samples have sampling distributions that are more skewed
questions.explanation: For i.i.d. observations with finite variance $\sigma^2$, $\bar{X}$ is approximately $N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)$ for large $n$, whatever the population shape. The raw data themselves keep the population's shape.

questions.text: Exam scores are normally distributed with mean 70 and standard deviation 10. Approximately what fraction of students score above 90?
options: About 2.3%
About 5%
About 16%
About 0.15%
questions.explanation: $z = (90 - 70)/10 = 2$ and $P(Z > 2) \approx 0.0228$. About 5% lie beyond $\pm 2\sigma$ in total, so only half of that is in the upper tail.

questions.text: The binomial distribution models:
options: The waiting time until the next event in a Poisson process
The number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials
The number of events in an interval with no fixed upper limit
The number of trials needed to obtain the first success
questions.explanation: A binomial count needs a fixed $n$, independent trials and a constant success probability $p$. The number of trials until the first success is geometric.

questions.text: Which of the following is a continuous distribution?
options: Poisson distribution
Binomial distribution
Normal distribution
Geometric distribution
questions.explanation: The normal distribution has a density over the whole real line. Poisson, binomial and geometric variables take only integer values.

questions.text: The cumulative distribution function (CDF) $F(x)$ of a random variable X gives:
options: $P(X = x)$, the probability of exactly the value x
$P(X \le x)$, the probability of a value at most x
$P(X > x)$, the probability of a value above x
$f(x)$, the height of the density at x
questions.explanation: By definition $F(x) = P(X \le x)$. The survival function is $1 - F(x) = P(X > x)$, and for a continuous variable the density is the derivative of $F$.

questions.text: Which statement is true for every normal distribution?
options: It is skewed to the right
It is bell-shaped and symmetric about its mean
It is used to model counts of events in an interval
It is restricted to non-negative values
questions.explanation: A normal density is symmetric about $\mu$, so its mean, median and mode coincide and its skewness is zero. It is defined on the whole real line.

questions.text: A help desk receives calls independently at an average rate of 4 per hour. Which distribution models the waiting time until the next call?
options: Normal distribution
Binomial distribution
Exponential distribution
Poisson distribution
questions.explanation: In a Poisson process the time between events is exponential with rate $\lambda = 4$ per hour, so the mean wait is $1/4$ hour. The Poisson distribution models the count, not the time.

questions.text: If $X \sim \text{Poisson}(2)$, what is $P(X = 0)$?
options: About 0.135
About 0.271
About 0.500
About 0.018
questions.explanation: $P(X = k) = e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$, so $P(X = 0) = e^{-2} \approx 0.135$. The value 0.271 is $P(X = 1) = 2e^{-2}$.

questions.text: For a Poisson distribution, as the rate parameter $\lambda$ increases, the distribution becomes:
options: More right-skewed
More symmetric and bell-shaped
Concentrated at zero
Narrower, with smaller variance
questions.explanation: The skewness of a Poisson distribution is $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$, which shrinks as $\lambda$ grows, so it approaches a normal shape. Its variance $\lambda$ grows, so it gets wider.

questions.text: In the notes' convention, what does a geometric random variable count?
options: The number of successes in a fixed number of trials
The waiting time between events in continuous time
The number of trials up to and including the first success
The number of trials needed to obtain r successes
questions.explanation: The notes define $X \sim \text{Geometric}(p)$ on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$ as the trial on which the first success occurs. Waiting for $r$ successes gives the negative binomial.

questions.text: Each trial succeeds independently with probability 0.2. What is the probability that the first success occurs on the third trial?
questions.explanation: The first two trials must fail and the third succeed: $P(X = 3) = (1-p)^2 p = 0.8^2 \times 0.2 = 0.128$.

questions.text: Which statement about the variance of a binomial distribution is true?
options: It always equals the number of trials n
It depends on both n and p, through $np(1-p)$
It does not depend on the success probability p
It is always less than 1
questions.explanation: $\text{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$, which for fixed $n$ is largest at $p = 0.5$. For example, $n = 100, p = 0.5$ gives variance 25.

questions.text: A fair coin is tossed 5 times. What is the probability of getting exactly 2 heads?
A Bernoulli random variable can take which two values?
options: −1 and 1
0 and 1
0 and any positive integer
Any two real numbers
questions.explanation: A Bernoulli variable records a single trial as 1 for success (probability $p$) and 0 for failure, so its mean is $p$ and its variance is $p(1-p)$.

questions.text: Which distribution counts the number of trials needed to obtain r successes in independent Bernoulli trials?
options: Geometric distribution
Negative binomial distribution
Binomial distribution
Poisson distribution
questions.explanation: The negative binomial generalises the geometric (which is the case $r = 1$). The binomial does the opposite: it fixes the number of trials and counts the successes.

questions.text: You want to model a proportion that varies between batches, such as the fraction of defective items, which must lie between 0 and 1. Which family is the natural choice?
options: Normal distribution
Exponential distribution
Beta distribution
Log-normal distribution
questions.explanation: The beta distribution is defined on $[0, 1]$ and its two shape parameters can make it flat, skewed or peaked. The other families give positive probability to values above 1.

questions.text: If waiting times are exponential with rate $\lambda = 0.5$ per minute, what is the probability of waiting more than 3 minutes?
options: About 0.22
About 0.78
About 0.50
About 0.05
questions.explanation: For an exponential variable $P(T > t) = e^{-\lambda t} = e^{-0.5 \times 3} = e^{-1.5} \approx 0.223$. The value 0.78 is $P(T \le 3)$.

questions.text: What is the null hypothesis in a two-sample t-test comparing two population means?
options: $H_0: \mu_1 \neq \mu_2$
$H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2$
questions.explanation: Hypotheses are statements about population parameters, and the null states no difference. A claim about sample means $\bar{x}_1, \bar{x}_2$ is not a hypothesis, since those are observed.

questions.text: Which test compares the variances of two normally distributed populations?
options: Independent-samples t-test
F-test for the ratio of two variances
Chi-square test of independence
Paired t-test
questions.explanation: Under $H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2$ the ratio $s_1^2/s_2^2$ follows an F distribution with $(n_1 - 1, n_2 - 1)$ degrees of freedom. This test is sensitive to non-normality.

questions.text: What does a 95% confidence level mean?
options: There is a 95% chance the null hypothesis is true
In repeated sampling, about 95% of intervals built this way contain the true parameter
There is a 95% probability the parameter lies in this particular computed interval
95% of the individual observations fall inside the interval
questions.explanation: The 95% describes the long-run success rate of the procedure. Once an interval is computed, the fixed parameter is either in it or not, and the interval is about the mean, not individual values.

questions.text: All else being equal, which change makes a confidence interval for a mean wider?
options: Lowering the confidence level from 95% to 90%
Decreasing the sample size
Reducing the population standard deviation
Increasing the sample size
questions.explanation: The margin of error is $z^* \sigma/\sqrt{n}$. A smaller $n$ increases the standard error. Lowering the confidence level, reducing $\sigma$ or increasing $n$ all make the interval narrower.

questions.text: What is the pooled variance in a two-sample t-test?
options: A weighted average of the two sample means
A weighted average of the two sample variances, weighted by degrees of freedom
The difference between the two sample variances
The sum of the two population variances
questions.explanation: $s_p^2 = \frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2 + (n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}$. It estimates the common variance under the equal-variance assumption.

questions.text: What feature of the study design calls for a paired t-test instead of an independent-samples t-test?
options: The two groups have equal variances
The data come from two unrelated sets of subjects
Each observation in one sample is matched to one in the other
Both samples contain more than 30 observations
questions.explanation: Paired designs, such as before-and-after measurements on the same subjects, produce dependent samples. The test analyses the within-pair differences, which removes between-subject variability.

questions.text: What does the Bonferroni correction adjust for?
options: Small sample sizes
Multiple comparisons, to control the family-wise error rate
Non-normal data distributions
Unequal variances between groups
questions.explanation: Testing each of $m$ hypotheses at level $\alpha/m$ keeps the probability of at least one false rejection at or below $\alpha$.

questions.text: Which non-parametric test is the usual alternative to the paired t-test?
options: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
Mann–Whitney U test
Kruskal–Wallis test
Chi-square goodness-of-fit test
questions.explanation: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test ranks the within-pair differences. Mann–Whitney U is the alternative for two independent samples, and Kruskal–Wallis for more than two independent groups.

questions.text: Which non-parametric test is the usual alternative to the independent-samples t-test?
options: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
Mann–Whitney U test
Friedman test
F-test for two variances
questions.explanation: The Mann–Whitney U test compares two independent samples using ranks. The signed-rank test is for paired data and Friedman's test is for three or more repeated measurements.

questions.text: What is the main advantage of a non-parametric hypothesis test?
options: It has more power than a t-test when the data are normal
It does not assume a specific distributional form for the data
It always gives narrower confidence intervals
It removes the need for independent observations
questions.explanation: Rank-based tests rely on fewer distributional assumptions, which helps with skewed data or outliers. When normality holds they are usually slightly less powerful, and they still assume independence.

questions.text: In a one-way ANOVA, what does a significant F-statistic indicate?
options: At least one group mean differs from the others
All the group means differ from each other
All the group variances are equal
The data are normally distributed
questions.explanation: ANOVA tests $H_0: \mu_1 = \dots = \mu_k$ against the alternative that not all means are equal. Finding out which means differ needs post-hoc comparisons.

questions.text: Which question is a chi-square test of independence designed to answer?
options: Do two independent groups have different means?
Is the correlation between two continuous variables zero?
Are two categorical variables associated in a contingency table?
Do three or more groups have different medians?
questions.explanation: The test compares observed cell counts with the counts expected if the row and column variables were independent. Mean comparisons use t-tests or ANOVA.

questions.text: Which change increases the power of a test, holding everything else fixed?
options: Decreasing the sample size
Raising the significance level from 0.01 to 0.05
Increasing the variability of the measurements
Testing for a smaller true effect
questions.explanation: A larger $\alpha$ enlarges the rejection region, so a false $H_0$ is rejected more often, at the cost of more Type I errors. The other three changes all reduce power.

questions.text: Two studies estimate the same mean with 95% intervals and the same sample standard deviation. Study A's interval is twice as wide as Study B's. What is the most likely reason?
options: Study A used about twice as many observations
Study A used about half as many observations
Study A used about a quarter as many observations
Study A used about four times as many observations
questions.explanation: Width is proportional to $s/\sqrt{n}$. Doubling the width requires $\sqrt{n}$ to halve, so $n_A \approx n_B/4$.

questions.text: Which test compares the means of two independent groups with roughly normal data?
options: Paired t-test
Independent-samples t-test
Chi-square test
Wilcoxon signed-rank test
questions.explanation: The independent-samples t-test is designed for two unrelated groups. A paired t-test needs matched observations, and chi-square tests are for categorical counts.

questions.text: What does the significance level α represent in hypothesis testing?
options: The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true
The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true
The p-value calculated from the sample
The probability of failing to reject a false null hypothesis
questions.explanation: $\alpha$ is the Type I error rate you choose before seeing the data. The probability of failing to reject a false null is $\beta$.

questions.text: Which condition justifies using a one-sample t-test for a mean?
options: The sample size must be larger than 100
The population variance must be known
The data come from a roughly normal population, or n is reasonably large
The data must be categorical
questions.explanation: The t-test estimates $\sigma$ with $s$ and relies on approximate normality, which the CLT provides for large $n$. A known population variance is the setting for a z-test.

questions.text: What does a p-value represent?
options: The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The probability, assuming $H_0$ is true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed
The probability that the result happened by chance alone
The significance level chosen for the test
questions.explanation: A p-value is computed under the assumption that $H_0$ holds. It is not the probability that $H_0$ is true, and it is not the probability that chance alone produced the result.

questions.text: For a test statistic with a symmetric null distribution, such as z or t, how is the two-tailed p-value computed?
options: As $P(T \ge t_{obs})$, the upper-tail area only
As $2P(T \ge |t_{obs}|)$, the area in both tails beyond $|t_{obs}|$
As $1 - P(T \ge |t_{obs}|)$, the central area
As $P(T \ge t_{obs})/2$, half the upper-tail area
questions.explanation: A two-tailed test treats departures in either direction as evidence against $H_0$, so it adds the two equal tail areas. That is twice the one-tailed p-value.

questions.text: A researcher wants to show that a new drug lowers mean systolic blood pressure below 140 mmHg. Which alternative hypothesis fits?
questions.explanation: A directional claim gives a one-tailed (left-tailed) alternative. The equality $\mu = 140$ belongs to the null hypothesis, and $\neq$ would be a two-tailed test.

questions.text: What does the null hypothesis $H_0$ usually represent?
options: No effect or no difference, the default claim being tested
The effect the researcher hopes to demonstrate
The claim that the sample mean exceeds the population mean
The claim that the p-value is below α
questions.explanation: $H_0$ is the status quo that the data must provide evidence against. The researcher's claim usually goes in the alternative $H_1$.

questions.text: When the p-value is less than or equal to α, what is the correct conclusion?
options: Fail to reject the null hypothesis
Accept the null hypothesis as proven
Reject the null hypothesis
Accept the alternative hypothesis as proven
questions.explanation: $p \le \alpha$ means the result would be unusual if $H_0$ were true, so $H_0$ is rejected. Rejection is evidence for $H_1$, not proof of it.

questions.text: What is the critical region of a hypothesis test?
options: The values of the statistic close to the hypothesised parameter
The set of test-statistic values for which $H_0$ is rejected
The set of values for which $H_0$ is proven true
The entire distribution of the sample data
questions.explanation: The critical (rejection) region has probability $\alpha$ under $H_0$ and lies in the tail or tails named by $H_1$. Values outside it lead to failing to reject, which does not prove $H_0$.

questions.text: A test gives p = 0.08 with α = 0.05. What is the correct conclusion?
options: Reject $H_0$; the result is statistically significant
Accept $H_0$; the null hypothesis has been shown to be true
Fail to reject $H_0$; the evidence against it is insufficient at this level
Reject $H_0$ because p is close to α
questions.explanation: Since $0.08 > 0.05$ we fail to reject $H_0$. That is not the same as showing $H_0$ is true: the study may simply lack power.

questions.text: In a paired t-test, which quantity is assumed to be approximately normally distributed?
options: The within-pair differences
The raw values in each group separately
The pooled values from both groups combined
The ranks of the observations
questions.explanation: A paired t-test is a one-sample t-test on the differences $d_i = x_i - y_i$, so normality is needed only for the differences.

questions.text: What does the standard error of the mean measure?
options: The spread of individual values in the population
The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$
The probability of a Type I error
The distance between the sample mean and the median
questions.explanation: $SE(\bar{x}) = \sigma/\sqrt{n}$ describes how much the sample mean varies from sample to sample. The population SD $\sigma$ describes individual values.

questions.text: What is a Type I error?
options: Rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true
Failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is false
Choosing a significance level that is too large
Using a one-tailed test when a two-tailed test was needed
questions.explanation: A Type I error is a false positive, and its probability is $\alpha$. Failing to reject a false null is a Type II error.

questions.text: Which outcome is a Type II error?
options: Rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true
Failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is false
Rejecting the null hypothesis when it is false
Failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is true
questions.explanation: A Type II error is a false negative, and its probability is $\beta$. Rejecting a false null and keeping a true null are both correct decisions.

questions.text: What is the power of a test?
options: The probability of rejecting $H_0$ when it is false
The probability of failing to reject $H_0$ when it is false
The probability of rejecting $H_0$ when it is true
The probability that $H_0$ is true given the data
questions.explanation: Power $= 1 - \beta$ is the chance of detecting a real effect. The second option is $\beta$ and the third is $\alpha$.

questions.text: What does the one-way ANOVA F-statistic compare?
options: The largest group mean with the smallest group mean
The between-group mean square with the within-group mean square
The variance of one group with the variance of another group
The observed cell counts with the expected cell counts
questions.explanation: $F = MST/MSE$. When the group means are equal both mean squares estimate $\sigma^2$, so $F \approx 1$. Large values suggest the means differ.

questions.text: A sample of $n = 36$ has mean $\bar{x} = 52$ and standard deviation $s = 6$. What is the t-statistic for testing $H_0: \mu = 50$?
questions.explanation: $t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}} = \frac{52 - 50}{6/\sqrt{36}} = \frac{2}{1} = 2.0$, with $n - 1 = 35$ degrees of freedom. Forgetting the $\sqrt{n}$ gives 0.33.

questions.text: A sample of $n = 25$ has mean 100, and the population standard deviation is known to be $\sigma = 15$. What is the 95% confidence interval for $\mu$?
questions.explanation: $SE = 15/\sqrt{25} = 3$ and the interval is $100 \pm 1.96 \times 3 = 100 \pm 5.88$. Using $z = 1.645$ would give the 90% interval (95.07, 104.93).

questions.text: A survey wants to halve the margin of error of a confidence interval for a mean, keeping the confidence level fixed. By what factor must the sample size grow?
options: $\sqrt{2}$
questions.explanation: The margin of error is proportional to $1/\sqrt{n}$. To halve it, $\sqrt{n}$ must double, so $n$ must quadruple.

questions.text: Roughly how much wider is a 99% z-interval than a 95% z-interval built from the same data?
options: About 1% wider
About 4% wider
About 31% wider
About twice as wide
questions.explanation: The width is proportional to the critical value, and $z_{0.995}/z_{0.975} = 2.576/1.960 \approx 1.31$. Higher confidence costs precision.

questions.text: In a poll of 100 people, 40 support a proposal. What is the approximate 95% margin of error for the population proportion?
questions.explanation: $SE = \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n} = \sqrt{0.4 \times 0.6/100} \approx 0.049$, and the margin is $1.96 \times 0.049 \approx 0.096$. The value 0.049 is the standard error alone.

questions.text: The 95% confidence interval for a difference in means $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ is $(-0.4, 3.2)$. What does a two-sided test of $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$ at α = 0.05 conclude?
options: Reject $H_0$, because most of the interval is positive
Fail to reject $H_0$, because the interval contains 0
Reject $H_0$, because the interval is wider than 3
The interval gives no information about the test
questions.explanation: A 95% interval contains exactly the null values that a two-sided test at $\alpha = 0.05$ would not reject. Since 0 is inside $(-0.4, 3.2)$, $H_0$ is not rejected.

questions.text: A two-sided z-test gives a statistic of z = 2.5. What is the p-value, approximately?
questions.explanation: $P(Z \ge 2.5) \approx 0.0062$, and a two-sided test doubles it: $2 \times 0.0062 \approx 0.0124$. The value 0.0062 is the one-sided p-value.

questions.text: A test has power 0.80. What is the probability of a Type II error for that effect size?
questions.explanation: Power $= 1 - \beta$, so $\beta = 1 - 0.80 = 0.20$. This is unrelated to $\alpha$, which governs Type I errors.

questions.text: A one-sample two-sided z-test at α = 0.05 should have power 0.80 to detect a shift of $\Delta = 5$ when $\sigma = 10$. About how many observations are needed?
questions.explanation: $n \approx (z_{0.975} + z_{0.80})^2\sigma^2/\Delta^2 = (1.96 + 0.84)^2 \times 100/25 \approx 31.4$, so round up to 32. The value 63 is the per-group size for a two-sample test.

questions.text: Group means are 105 and 100, and the pooled standard deviation is 10. What is Cohen's d?
questions.explanation: $d = (\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2)/s_p = 5/10 = 0.5$, conventionally a medium effect. Effect size describes magnitude, which a p-value does not.

questions.text: A trial with 200,000 participants finds that a drug lowers blood pressure by 0.3 mmHg, with p < 0.001. What is the best interpretation?
options: The effect must be clinically important because p is tiny
The effect is statistically significant but may be too small to matter
The p-value shows there is a 99.9% chance the drug works
The result is a Type I error because the effect is small
questions.explanation: With huge samples even trivial effects give tiny p-values. Statistical significance is not practical significance, so the effect size must be judged on its own.

questions.text: If 10 independent tests are each run at α = 0.05 and all null hypotheses are true, what is the probability of at least one false rejection?
options: About 0.40
About 0.005
questions.explanation: $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - (1 - 0.05)^{10} = 1 - 0.95^{10} \approx 0.401$. This inflation of the family-wise error rate is the multiple-comparisons problem.

questions.text: A study runs 10 tests and wants the family-wise error rate at most 0.05. What per-test threshold does the Bonferroni correction use?
questions.explanation: Bonferroni tests each hypothesis at $\alpha/m = 0.05/10 = 0.005$. It is simple but conservative, so it can miss real effects.

questions.text: Five tests give ordered p-values 0.001, 0.012, 0.020, 0.041, 0.300. Using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure at FDR level 0.05, how many hypotheses are rejected?
questions.explanation: Compare $p_{(i)}$ with $\frac{i}{5}(0.05)$: 0.001 ≤ 0.01, 0.012 ≤ 0.02, 0.020 ≤ 0.03, but 0.041 > 0.04 and 0.300 > 0.05. The largest passing rank is 3, so the three smallest are rejected.

questions.text: How does controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) differ from controlling the family-wise error rate (FWER)?
options: FDR limits the probability of making any false rejection at all
FDR limits the expected proportion of false rejections among all rejections
FDR limits the probability of a Type II error in each test
FDR applies only when exactly two hypotheses are tested
questions.explanation: FWER control (e.g. Bonferroni, Holm) bounds the chance of even one false positive. FDR control (e.g. Benjamini–Hochberg) tolerates some false positives, which gives more power when many tests are run.

questions.text: What are the degrees of freedom for a chi-square test of independence on a 3 × 4 contingency table?
questions.explanation: $df = (r-1)(c-1) = (3-1)(4-1) = 6$. The 11 would be $rc - 1$, which ignores that the row and column totals are fixed.

questions.text: In a contingency table with grand total 200, a cell's row total is 60 and its column total is 50. What is its expected count under independence?
questions.explanation: $E = \frac{\text{row total} \times \text{column total}}{\text{grand total}} = \frac{60 \times 50}{200} = 15$.

questions.text: A coin is tossed 50 times and lands heads 30 times. What is the chi-square goodness-of-fit statistic for testing that the coin is fair?
questions.explanation: The expected counts are 25 and 25, so $\chi^2 = \frac{(30-25)^2}{25} + \frac{(20-25)^2}{25} = 1 + 1 = 2.0$, with $df = 1$. This is below the 0.05 critical value 3.84.

questions.text: Which condition is commonly required for the chi-square approximation to be reliable?
options: Every observed count is at least 30
The expected counts are large enough, typically at least 5 per cell
The data are normally distributed within each category
The row and column totals are all equal
questions.explanation: The chi-square distribution is a large-sample approximation that depends on expected counts, not observed ones. With small expected counts, combine categories or use an exact test.

questions.text: A one-way ANOVA compares k = 4 groups with N = 40 observations in total. What are the degrees of freedom of the F-statistic?
questions.explanation: The numerator (between groups) has $k - 1 = 3$ df and the denominator (within groups) has $N - k = 36$ df. The total df is $N - 1 = 39$.

questions.text: A one-way ANOVA with 3 groups and 30 observations has SSB = 60 and SSW = 270. What is the F-statistic?
questions.explanation: $MSB = 60/(3-1) = 30$ and $MSW = 270/(30-3) = 10$, so $F = 30/10 = 3.0$ on (2, 27) df. Dividing the raw sums of squares would give 0.22.

questions.text: Why is one-way ANOVA preferred over running a t-test for every pair of five groups?
options: Pairwise t-tests cannot handle more than two groups at once
Ten separate tests at α = 0.05 inflate the overall chance of a false positive
ANOVA does not require any assumptions about the data
ANOVA tells you directly which pairs of means differ
questions.explanation: Five groups give $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ pairwise tests, so the family-wise error rate is far above 0.05. ANOVA tests all means at once; post-hoc methods then identify which pairs differ.

questions.text: After a significant one-way ANOVA, which method compares all pairs of group means while controlling the family-wise error rate?
options: Levene's test
Tukey's honest significant difference (HSD)
Chi-square test of independence
Shapiro–Wilk test
questions.explanation: Tukey's HSD is a post-hoc procedure for all pairwise comparisons. Levene's test checks equal variances and Shapiro–Wilk checks normality, both of which are assumption checks.

questions.text: What are the degrees of freedom for a one-sample t-test with n = 16 observations?
questions.explanation: Estimating the mean uses up one degree of freedom, so $df = n - 1 = 15$. The two-tailed 5% critical value is then about 2.131.

questions.text: Why does a t-interval use a larger critical value than a z-interval at the same confidence level?
options: Because the sample mean is biased when σ is unknown
Because estimating σ with s adds uncertainty, giving the t distribution heavier tails
Because the t distribution is skewed to the right
Because t-intervals are used only for large samples
questions.explanation: The t distribution accounts for the extra variability of $s$. Its tails are heavier than the normal's for small $df$ and it approaches $N(0,1)$ as $df$ grows.

questions.text: Which version of the two-sample t-test should you use when the two groups appear to have clearly unequal variances?
options: Pooled-variance t-test
Welch's t-test
Paired t-test
One-sample t-test
questions.explanation: Welch's test uses separate variance estimates and approximate degrees of freedom, so it does not rely on equal variances. The pooled test assumes $\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2$.

questions.text: In a paired study of 25 subjects, the differences have mean 1.5 and standard deviation 3. What is the paired t-statistic?
questions.explanation: $t = \frac{\bar{d}}{s_d/\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.5}{3/\sqrt{25}} = \frac{1.5}{0.6} = 2.5$ on 24 df. Omitting $\sqrt{n}$ gives 0.5.

questions.text: What is a time series?
options: A random sample of independent observations from a population
A sequence of observations of a variable indexed in time order
A type of linear regression model with lagged predictors
A set of measurements on many units taken at one moment
questions.explanation: What makes data a time series is the time ordering, usually at regular intervals. Nearby observations are typically dependent, unlike an i.i.d. sample. Measurements on many units at one moment are cross-sectional data.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of seasonality?
options: A gradual upward trend in sales over several years
Sales peaking every December because of holiday shopping
A one-time spike in sales caused by a special event
Day-to-day random fluctuations in a stock price
questions.explanation: Seasonality is a pattern that repeats with a fixed, known period, here 12 months. A long-run drift is a trend and a one-off spike is an outlier or intervention.

questions.text: What is first differencing, $y_t - y_{t-1}$, mainly used for?
options: Removing a repeating pattern with a period of 12
Removing a trend or unit root so the mean becomes stationary
Stabilising a variance that grows with the level of the series
Smoothing out high-frequency noise for plotting
questions.explanation: Differencing turns a random walk or a linear trend into a series with a stable mean. Seasonal patterns need lag-$m$ differencing, and a variance that grows with the level calls for a log or Box–Cox transform.

questions.text: In an ARIMA(p, d, q) model, what does d represent?
options: The number of autoregressive terms
The number of differences needed to make the series stationary
The number of moving-average terms
The length of the seasonal period
questions.explanation: The "I" (integrated) part applies $(1 - B)^d$ before an ARMA(p, q) is fitted. Most series need $d = 0$, 1 or occasionally 2.

questions.text: Which plot is most useful for choosing the AR order p of an ARIMA model?
options: Partial autocorrelation function (PACF)
Autocorrelation function (ACF)
Histogram of the residuals
Seasonal decomposition plot
questions.explanation: For an AR(p) process the theoretical PACF cuts off after lag $p$. The ACF cutting off after lag $q$ is the signature of an MA(q).

questions.text: What is the main purpose of seasonal differencing $y_t - y_{t-m}$ in a SARIMA model?
options: To stabilise the variance of the series
To remove a non-seasonal linear trend only
To remove a recurring seasonal pattern of period m
To smooth random noise between seasons
questions.explanation: Subtracting the value from the same season one cycle earlier removes a stable seasonal pattern. In the model this is the $(1 - B^m)^D$ factor.

questions.text: In a SARIMA(p, d, q)×(P, D, Q)m model, what does P control?
options: The number of seasonal autoregressive terms
The order of seasonal differencing
The number of seasonal moving-average terms
The number of non-seasonal moving-average terms
questions.explanation: Uppercase letters are the seasonal counterparts of p, d and q. $P$ is the order of the seasonal AR polynomial $\Phi(B^m)$, with lags at multiples of $m$.

questions.text: Which criterion balances goodness of fit against model complexity when comparing ARIMA models?
options: The maximised log-likelihood alone
AIC (Akaike information criterion)
Durbin–Watson statistic
questions.explanation: $AIC = -2\log L + 2k$ rewards fit and penalises the number of parameters $k$. The log-likelihood alone always favours bigger models.

questions.text: What typically happens if a random walk is differenced twice instead of once?
options: The series keeps a unit root and remains non-stationary
A strong negative lag-1 autocorrelation appears and the variance increases
All autocorrelation is removed and the series becomes white noise
The AIC of any model fitted to the series always decreases
questions.explanation: Over-differencing white noise gives $\varepsilon_t - \varepsilon_{t-1}$, an MA(1) with lag-1 autocorrelation $-0.5$ and twice the variance. It adds structure and noise rather than removing it.

questions.text: After fitting an ARIMA model, which diagnostic suggests the residuals are still autocorrelated?
options: A Shapiro–Wilk test that rejects normality
Several significant spikes in the ACF of the residuals
A roughly constant residual variance over time
A Ljung–Box p-value of 0.40
questions.explanation: Residuals from an adequate model should look like white noise. A large Ljung–Box p-value (such as 0.40) fails to reject that, while ACF spikes outside the bounds point to structure the model missed.

questions.text: A series behaves like a random walk with drift. Which operation makes it stationary?
options: Taking logarithms of the series
Taking first differences
Taking lag-12 seasonal differences only
Applying a 3-point moving average
questions.explanation: For $y_t = \delta + y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$, the first difference $\Delta y_t = \delta + \varepsilon_t$ is stationary. Logs and moving averages leave the unit root in place.

questions.text: How does an LSTM differ from a basic recurrent neural network (RNN) in time series forecasting?
options: An LSTM uses moving averages of past values instead of the values themselves
An LSTM uses gated memory cells that help it learn long-range dependencies
An LSTM requires the series to be stationary while an RNN does not
An LSTM can only be applied to strongly seasonal data
questions.explanation: LSTM gates control what is stored and forgotten, which improves gradient flow and eases the vanishing-gradient problem of plain RNNs. Like other models, LSTMs still need chronological evaluation.

questions.text: Which is the usual way to fill a few missing values in a smooth time series?
options: Drop the entire series from the analysis
Replace them with the mean of the whole series
Interpolate between neighbours, or carry the last value forward
Replace them with randomly chosen observed values
questions.explanation: Interpolation and forward or backward fill use nearby observations, which respects the time dependence. A global mean ignores trend and seasonality and can create artificial jumps.

questions.text: Which evaluation scheme respects temporal ordering when assessing a forecasting model?
options: Random k-fold cross-validation
Leave-one-out cross-validation on shuffled data
Rolling-origin (time series) cross-validation
Bootstrapping individual observations
questions.explanation: Rolling-origin evaluation always trains on the past and tests on the following period, as in real forecasting. Random folds leak future information into training.

questions.text: What is the key difference between ARIMA and SARIMA models?
options: ARIMA includes seasonal terms and SARIMA does not
SARIMA never requires any differencing
SARIMA adds seasonal AR, differencing and MA terms at lags that are multiples of m
ARIMA can model only additive components
questions.explanation: SARIMA multiplies the non-seasonal ARIMA polynomials by seasonal ones, $\Phi(B^m)$, $(1-B^m)^D$ and $\Theta(B^m)$, to capture repeating patterns of period $m$.

questions.text: A standard classical decomposition splits a time series into which components?
options: Autoregressive, integrated and moving-average parts
Trend, autocorrelation and residual
Trend(-cycle), seasonal and remainder (noise)
Mean, median and mode
questions.explanation: Decomposition writes $y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t$ (additive) or $y_t = T_t \times S_t \times R_t$ (multiplicative). Methods such as STL estimate the components with local smoothing.

questions.text: Which metric measures the average absolute percentage error of forecasts?
options: MAE (mean absolute error)
MSE (mean squared error)
RMSE (root mean squared error)
MAPE (mean absolute percentage error)
questions.explanation: $MAPE = \frac{100}{n}\sum |e_t / y_t|$ expresses errors relative to the actual values, so it is scale-free. MAE and RMSE are in the units of the data.

questions.text: When is MAPE a poor choice of forecast accuracy measure?
options: When the series is measured in different units from another series
When some actual values are zero or very close to zero
When forecasts are compared across several horizons
When the errors are symmetric around zero
questions.explanation: MAPE divides by $y_t$, so it is undefined at zero and explodes near zero. Scaled measures such as MASE avoid this.

questions.text: What does m denote in SARIMA(p, d, q)×(P, D, Q)m?
options: The order of the non-seasonal MA terms
The total number of model parameters
The seasonal period, such as 12 for monthly data
The number of differences applied
questions.explanation: $m$ is the number of observations per seasonal cycle, such as 12 for monthly data with yearly seasonality or 4 for quarterly data. The seasonal terms act at lags $m, 2m, \dots$

questions.text: Why do ARIMA prediction intervals widen as the forecast horizon grows?
options: The model's parameters change over time
Uncertainty from future shocks accumulates with each step ahead
Seasonality becomes stronger at longer lags
The residuals become more autocorrelated over time
questions.explanation: Each future step adds an unknown innovation. For a random walk the $h$-step forecast error variance is $h\sigma^2$, so the interval width grows like $\sqrt{h}$.

questions.text: What is the null hypothesis of the augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) test?
options: The series is stationary
The series has a unit root, so it is non-stationary
The residuals are normally distributed
The autocorrelations at all lags are zero
questions.explanation: The ADF test checks $H_0: \gamma = 0$ in $\Delta X_t = \alpha + \gamma X_{t-1} + \dots$, which means a unit root. A small p-value is evidence for stationarity.

questions.text: Which property defines a weakly stationary time series?
options: Its mean and variance change over time
Constant mean and variance, and autocovariances that depend only on the lag
A strong seasonal component with a fixed period
An increasing deterministic trend
questions.explanation: Weak stationarity requires $E[X_t] = \mu$, $\text{Var}(X_t) = \sigma^2$ and $\text{Cov}(X_t, X_{t+h}) = \gamma(h)$ for all $t$. Trends and seasonality violate it.

questions.text: What does the autocorrelation function (ACF) measure?
options: The correlation between a series and lagged copies of itself
The long-run trend in the series
The correlation between two different time series
The forecast accuracy of a fitted model
questions.explanation: $\rho(h) = \gamma(h)/\gamma(0)$ is the correlation between $X_t$ and $X_{t+h}$. The correlation between two different series at various lags is the cross-correlation function.

questions.text: In time series analysis, what is a lag?
options: A delay in collecting the data
The difference between actual and predicted values
An earlier value of the same series, such as $y_{t-k}$
A type of error in the fitted model
questions.explanation: Lag $k$ refers to the value $k$ periods back, so $B^k y_t = y_{t-k}$. ACFs and AR models are built on lagged values.

questions.text: What is a simple moving average used as a smoothing tool?
options: The unweighted average of the most recent k observations
The long-run average of the entire series
The average of a model's forecasted values
A weighted sum of past forecast errors
questions.explanation: $SMA_t = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} y_{t-i}$ smooths short-term noise. It is different from an MA(q) model, which is a weighted sum of past innovations.

questions.text: What is the main difference between an AR model and an MA model?
options: AR models use past values of the series; MA models use past innovations (shocks)
AR models are for stationary series; MA models are for non-stationary series
AR models predict future values; MA models only smooth the data
AR models capture seasonality; MA models capture trend
questions.explanation: AR(p): $X_t = c + \sum \phi_i X_{t-i} + \varepsilon_t$. MA(q): $X_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t + \sum \theta_j \varepsilon_{t-j}$. Both can be used for forecasting.

questions.text: What does the partial autocorrelation function (PACF) measure at lag k?
options: The total correlation between the series and its lag-k value
The correlation between $X_t$ and $X_{t-k}$ after removing the effect of lags 1 to k−1
The residuals of a fitted time series model
The difference between actual and forecasted values
questions.explanation: The PACF isolates the direct relationship at lag $k$. For an AR(p) process it is zero beyond lag $p$.

questions.text: Which model is the simplest that has both autoregressive and moving-average components for a stationary, non-seasonal series?
options: ARMA(p, q)
AR(p)
MA(q)
Random walk
questions.explanation: ARMA combines $p$ AR terms and $q$ MA terms. ARIMA adds differencing and SARIMA adds seasonal terms, so both build on ARMA.

questions.text: What is the null hypothesis of the KPSS test?
options: The series is (level or trend) stationary
The series has a unit root
The residuals have constant variance
Past values of another series do not help prediction
questions.explanation: KPSS reverses the ADF set-up, which is why the two are often used together. Rejecting KPSS while failing to reject ADF is consistent evidence of a unit root.

questions.text: What is the optimal point forecast $\hat{y}_{T+h}$ for a random walk without drift?
options: The mean of all past observations
The last observed value $y_T$, for every horizon h
Zero, for every horizon h
$y_T$ plus h times the average past change
questions.explanation: Because $y_{t} = y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$ with zero-mean shocks, the best forecast is the current level. This is the naive forecast. Adding $h\delta$ applies only to a random walk with drift.

questions.text: For a random walk with innovation variance $\sigma^2$, what is the variance of the h-step-ahead forecast error?
options: $\sigma^2$, the same at every horizon
$h\sigma^2$
$h^2\sigma^2$
$\sigma^2 / h$
questions.explanation: The $h$-step error is the sum of $h$ independent shocks, so its variance is $h\sigma^2$. Intervals therefore widen in proportion to $\sqrt{h}$.

questions.text: Monthly sales show a trend and a stable seasonal pattern. Which exponential smoothing method is designed for this?
options: Simple exponential smoothing
Holt's linear trend method
Holt–Winters (triple) exponential smoothing
A simple moving average
