questions.explanation: Holt–Winters adds a seasonal equation to Holt's level and trend equations. Simple exponential smoothing handles neither trend nor seasonality, and Holt's method handles only trend.

questions.text: For which values of $\phi$ is the AR(1) model $X_t = \phi X_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$ stationary?
options: $\phi > 1$
Any value of $\phi$
questions.explanation: With $|\phi| < 1$ shocks die out geometrically. $\phi = 1$ gives a random walk (a unit root) and $|\phi| > 1$ makes the series explode.

questions.text: What does the p parameter in ARIMA(p, d, q) control?
options: The number of lagged values included (the AR order)
The number of differences applied
The number of lagged forecast errors (the MA order)
The order of seasonal differencing
questions.explanation: $p$ is the degree of the AR polynomial $\phi(B) = 1 - \phi_1 B - \dots - \phi_p B^p$, so $p$ past values enter the model.

questions.text: A stationary AR(1) process has $\phi = 0.6$. What is its theoretical lag-2 autocorrelation $\rho(2)$?
questions.explanation: For AR(1), $\rho(h) = \phi^h$, so $\rho(2) = 0.6^2 = 0.36$. The ACF decays geometrically rather than cutting off.

questions.text: A sample ACF has significant spikes at lags 1 and 2 and then cuts off, while the PACF tails off gradually. Which model does this suggest?
options: AR(2)
MA(2)
ARMA(2, 2)
White noise
questions.explanation: An MA(q) process has an ACF that cuts off after lag $q$ and a PACF that tails off. An AR(2) would show the reverse: a PACF cut-off after lag 2.

questions.text: What is the mean of the stationary AR(1) process $X_t = 2 + 0.6X_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$?
questions.explanation: Taking expectations, $\mu = 2 + 0.6\mu$, so $\mu = c/(1-\phi) = 2/0.4 = 5$. The constant $c$ is not the mean unless $\phi = 0$.

questions.text: An AR(1) process has $\phi = 0.6$ and innovation variance $\sigma^2_\varepsilon = 1$. What is its variance?
questions.explanation: $\text{Var}(X_t) = \sigma^2_\varepsilon/(1 - \phi^2) = 1/(1 - 0.36) = 1/0.64 = 1.5625$. The value 2.5 comes from dividing by $1 - \phi$ instead.

questions.text: When is the MA(1) model $X_t = \varepsilon_t + \theta\varepsilon_{t-1}$ invertible?
options: For every value of $\theta$
When $|\theta| < 1$
When $|\theta| > 1$
When $\theta = 1$
questions.explanation: With $|\theta| < 1$ the innovations can be recovered as a convergent weighted sum of current and past observations. Invertibility also picks a unique MA model from pairs with the same ACF.

questions.text: Using the backward shift operator, what is $(1 - B)^2 y_t$?
questions.explanation: $(1 - B)^2 = 1 - 2B + B^2$, and $B^k y_t = y_{t-k}$. This is the second difference. Note that $y_t - y_{t-2}$ is $(1 - B^2)y_t$, a lag-2 difference.

questions.text: A monthly series is modelled with SARIMA(1,1,1)×(1,1,1)12. How many initial observations are lost to differencing?
questions.explanation: The combined operator $(1 - B)(1 - B^{12})$ reaches back $d + Dm = 1 + 12 = 13$ periods, so the first 13 values have no differenced counterpart.

questions.text: What is the null hypothesis of the Ljung–Box test applied to model residuals?
options: The residuals have a unit root
The residual autocorrelations up to the tested lag are jointly zero
The residuals are normally distributed
The residual variance is constant over time
questions.explanation: $Q_{LB} = n(n+2)\sum_{h=1}^{m}\hat{\rho}(h)^2/(n-h)$ is compared with a $\chi^2$ distribution. A small p-value means serial correlation remains in the residuals.

questions.text: Two ARIMA models are fitted to the same data. Model A has BIC 412.3 and model B has BIC 405.8. Which is preferred by BIC?
options: Model A, because its BIC is higher
Model B, because its BIC is lower
Neither, because BIC values cannot be compared
The model with more parameters, whatever its BIC
questions.explanation: Lower information criteria are better. BIC penalises parameters with $k \ln n$, more heavily than AIC, so it favours parsimonious models. Comparisons are valid only on the same data and with the same differencing.

questions.text: What defines a white noise process?
options: Zero mean, constant variance and no autocorrelation at any non-zero lag
A linear trend plus random fluctuations
Observations that are positively correlated with their previous values
A strong seasonal component with random amplitude
questions.explanation: White noise has $E[\varepsilon_t] = 0$, $\text{Var}(\varepsilon_t) = \sigma^2$ and $\text{Cov}(\varepsilon_t, \varepsilon_s) = 0$ for $t \neq s$. It is the benchmark that good model residuals should resemble.

questions.text: How does simple exponential smoothing form its forecast?
options: As a weighted average of past observations with exponentially decreasing weights
As an equally weighted average of all past observations
By fitting a straight-line trend to the whole series
By regressing the series on its own lag-1 value
questions.explanation: $\hat{y}_{t+1} = \alpha y_t + (1 - \alpha)\hat{y}_t$, so the weight on $y_{t-j}$ is $\alpha(1 - \alpha)^j$. A larger $\alpha$ reacts faster to recent changes.

questions.text: In time series forecasting, what does overfitting mean?
options: Using too few observations to fit the model
A model fits the training period closely but forecasts new periods poorly
A model that ignores the seasonality in the data
Smoothing the data so much that real patterns are lost
questions.explanation: An overfit model captures noise specific to the training sample, such as too many ARMA terms. Its in-sample errors look small while its out-of-sample errors are large.

questions.text: Actual values are 10, 12 and 8, and the forecasts are 11, 10 and 8. What are the MAE and RMSE?
options: MAE 1.0, RMSE about 1.29
MAE 1.0, RMSE 1.0
MAE 1.5, RMSE about 1.67
MAE 0.33, RMSE about 1.29
questions.explanation: The errors are −1, 2 and 0. MAE $= (1 + 2 + 0)/3 = 1.0$ and RMSE $= \sqrt{(1 + 4 + 0)/3} = \sqrt{5/3} \approx 1.29$. RMSE ≥ MAE, because squaring weights the larger error more.

questions.text: What does the Box–Jenkins methodology focus on?
options: An iterative cycle of identifying, estimating and checking ARIMA models
Decomposing a series into seasonal components only
Smoothing a series with moving averages
Running hypothesis tests on the means of time series
questions.explanation: Box–Jenkins uses ACF and PACF to identify a model, then estimates it and checks its residuals. If the diagnostics fail, the cycle repeats before the model is used for forecasting.

questions.text: Daily stock returns show little autocorrelation, but large moves tend to be followed by large moves. Which model family targets this volatility clustering?
options: Seasonal ARIMA models
ARCH and GARCH models
Holt's linear trend method
Simple moving averages
questions.explanation: GARCH models let the conditional variance depend on past squared shocks and past variances, so volatility persists. The ACF of squared returns, not raw returns, reveals the effect.

questions.text: In a VAR model, what does it mean that x Granger-causes y?
options: Changes in x are proven to cause changes in y
Past values of x improve predictions of y beyond y's own past
x and y are perfectly correlated at lag 0
y has a unit root while x is stationary
questions.explanation: Granger causality is about predictive information: it tests whether the lagged-x coefficients in y's equation are jointly zero. It does not establish true causation.

questions.text: A periodogram of a monthly series has its largest peak at frequency 1/12 ≈ 0.083 cycles per month. What does this indicate?
options: A cycle that repeats 12 times per month
A cycle with a period of about 12 months
A linear trend with slope 0.083
Autocorrelation of 0.083 at lag 12
questions.explanation: Period is the reciprocal of frequency, so $1/(1/12) = 12$ months, an annual pattern. The notes stress converting a peak's frequency back to a period before interpreting it.

questions.text: What does the Kalman filter do in a linear Gaussian state-space model?
options: It removes seasonality by differencing at lag m
It recursively updates the estimate of an unobserved state as each observation arrives
It selects ARIMA orders by minimising AIC
It tests whether the series has a unit root
questions.explanation: At each step the filter predicts the state, compares the prediction with the new observation, and corrects it using the Kalman gain. The gain weighs the prediction's uncertainty against the observation's.

questions.text: A series' fluctuations grow in proportion to its level. Which transformation is commonly applied before fitting an ARIMA model?
options: Seasonal differencing at lag 12
A log or Box–Cox transformation
Adding a constant to every observation
Removing every second observation
questions.explanation: Logs turn multiplicative variation into additive variation, which stabilises the variance. Differencing deals with the mean, not with a variance that grows with the level.
